body:
Trump Admin lets BlackRock dramatically expand utility ownership even as it pushes for double-digit rate increases

In just over a year, BlackRock has secured utilities serving nearly 9 million people, raising concerns about higher electricity bills.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) approved BlackRock’s $33.4 billion takeover of AES Corporation on Tuesday, clearing the final required regulatory approval for an acquisition that will place major electric utilities in Indiana and Ohio under private equity ownership. AES announced that the transaction is expected to close December 2.

The decision comes despite concerns raised by the Private Equity Stakeholder Project (PESP), Public Citizen, and Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana about BlackRock’s growing influence over U.S. utilities and the potential consequences for electricity customers. The groups filed a joint protest challenging BlackRock’s expanding utility holdings and raising questions about its existing federal investment authorizations.

The independent market monitor for PJM, the regional electricity market serving AES Ohio, also warned that the acquisition could increase market power and undermine competition. Former FERC Commissioner Mark Christie similarly warned that large asset managers’ utility holdings pose the threat of “decreased innovation, reduced competition, and ultimately higher prices to consumers.”

In a letter to FERC, Senator Elizabeth Warren and a bipartisan group of House members wrote:

“GIP’s application fails to establish how this merger is consistent with the public interest and leaves open the possibility that the merger could be used to cross-subsidize other non-utility lines of BlackRock’s businesses, all while unfairly passing on transaction costs to their consumers. Based on our review of the application filed by BlackRock’s GIP and its co-applicants, we urge FERC to deny the merger.”

FERC declined to reconsider BlackRock’s existing blanket authorization as part of the AES proceeding and rejected requests for additional conditions addressing competition concerns.

“FERC had an opportunity to scrutinize BlackRock’s growing control over the electricity system, but instead gave this takeover the green light,” said Nichole Heil, senior research and campaign coordinator at PESP. “The concerns about competition and higher electricity bills aren’t going away just because the deal has been approved.”

The acquisition will significantly expand the consortium’s energy holdings. According to PESP’s research, the deal will nearly double BlackRock’s fossil fuel power plant portfolio to 50 plants, with an estimated 32,000 megawatts of generating capacity across 11 countries. EQT’s power plant portfolio will grow from 10 to 37 plants. Between AES and Minnesota Power’s parent company, ALLETE, BlackRock will have financial interests in utilities serving more than 8.8 million people.

The approval comes just weeks after BlackRock-owned Minnesota Power requested a 17.8% rate increase, totaling $134 million annually, one day after a one-year rate freeze expired. During Minnesota’s acquisition review in 2025, an administrative law judge recommended rejecting the takeover after reviewing investors’ financial projections and warning about the risk of significant rate increases.

With the AES acquisition now cleared to proceed, attention turns to ongoing utility rate proceedings in Indiana and Ohio. Indiana regulators have reopened AES Indiana’s $71 million electricity rate case amid the pending acquisition and the appointment of a new commission chair. In Ohio, regulators have already approved the acquisition, and AES Ohio recently sought a $143 million rate increase.

The investors seeking to acquire AES are targeting returns substantially higher than those historically generated by regulated utilities. PESP has warned that these expectations raise questions about how the acquisition’s financial benefits will be generated and whether customers could face pressure to pay higher rates.

“BlackRock’s Minnesota Power takeover is already raising serious questions about who will pay for Wall Street’s profits,” said Heil. “As soon as its temporary rate freeze ended, the utility asked customers to pay nearly 18% more. Indiana and Ohio regulators should be asking where BlackRock’s promised investor returns will come from and who will ultimately pay for them.”

FERC’s approval does not determine future retail electricity rates. Those decisions remain subject to the relevant regulatory proceedings, where the financial consequences of private equity ownership will continue to be scrutinized.
